steps: Choose sampling type: random, systematic, or stratified
Decide sample size: larger = more reliable
Collect data consistently at each point
Check for anomalies that don't fit the pattern
method_card.title: Sampling & Fieldwork Data
method_card.content:
In geography fieldwork, you cannot measure everything — so you take a sample. The sampling method you choose affects how reliable and representative your results are.

Random sampling: Every point has an equal chance of being selected (e.g. using random number generators to pick grid coordinates). Reduces bias but may miss important features.

Systematic sampling: Measurements taken at regular intervals (e.g. every 50 metres along a river, every 5th house). Easy to carry out and gives good coverage, but may miss patterns that repeat at the same interval.

Stratified sampling: The study area is divided into sub-groups (strata) and samples are taken proportionally from each (e.g. sampling different land use zones separately). Ensures all groups are represented but requires advance knowledge of the area.

Anomalies are data points that don't fit the overall pattern — they may be caused by measurement error, unusual local conditions, or human interference. Identify them by looking for values far above or below the trend. Don't automatically remove them — investigate the cause first.

Reliability increases with larger sample sizes, consistent methods, and repeated measurements. Bias is reduced by choosing appropriate sampling strategies.
method_card.example:
Scenario: A student is studying how river velocity changes downstream. She measures velocity at 10 equally-spaced points from source to mouth.

Sampling method: This is systematic sampling — measurements at regular intervals (every X metres).

Why systematic? It gives even coverage of the whole river course, ensuring upstream and downstream are both represented.

Anomaly check: If one reading (e.g. 0.1 m/s in the lower course where all others are 1.5+ m/s) is very different, it may be an anomaly caused by a weir, bridge, or measurement error.

gold.hint: Grid squares are numbered 1–200. Reject any numbers outside this range.
gold.display: A study area is divided into 200 grid squares. A student uses a random number table and gets these numbers: 7, 156, 203, 42, 89, 301, 12, 178. How many of these are valid grid square selections?

misconceptions.message: Grid squares run 1–200. Numbers 203 and 301 exceed 200, so they're invalid. Valid: 7, 156, 42, 89, 12, 178 = 6 selections.

gold.hint: Original total = mean × n. Subtract the anomaly, divide by n − 1
gold.display: A river study collects velocity data at 15 sites. The mean velocity is 1.2 m/s. One reading of 8.5 m/s is identified as an anomaly (equipment malfunction). What is the corrected mean if this reading is removed? Give to 2 decimal places.

misconceptions.message: After removing one value, divide by 14 (not 15): 9.5 ÷ 14 ≈ 0.68.

gold.display: A student needs to survey 80 people in a town. The town has: young adults (18–30) = 25%, middle-aged (31–55) = 45%, elderly (56+) = 30%. Using stratified sampling, how many middle-aged people should be surveyed?

misconceptions.message: Stratified = proportional to population share. Middle-aged = 45% of 80 = 36 people.

gold.hint: Range = max − min. Mean = sum ÷ 5. Then (range ÷ mean) × 100
gold.display: A student collects environmental quality data and calculates the mean score for 5 sites: 14, 12, 16, 13, 15. She wants to check reliability by calculating the range as a percentage of the mean. What is this percentage? Round to 1 decimal place.
Explain why random sampling might be impractical for a river study measuring velocity at different points along a 5 km river course, even though it reduces bias.
options: Random points might all cluster in one section, leaving large stretches unmeasured — missing the downstream trend the study aims to show
The river is too short for random sampling
Random sampling requires more than 100 sample points

misconceptions.message: Random sampling is often practical. The specific issue here is that randomly chosen points might cluster together, leaving parts of the river unsampled — bad for studying a downstream trend.
5 km is long enough. The problem is that random points may not give even coverage, potentially missing the spatial trend downstream.

bronze.display: A student measures soil temperature every 10 metres along a 100 m transect across a field. What type of sampling is this?

misconceptions.message: Measurements at regular intervals (every 10 m) is systematic sampling, not random. Random would use random number generators to choose points.
Stratified sampling divides the area into groups first. Regular-interval measurement is systematic sampling.

bronze.display: A student uses a random number table to pick 20 grid squares for a land use survey. What type of sampling is this?

misconceptions.message: Using random number tables gives every point an equal chance — this is random sampling. Systematic would use regular intervals.
There's no division into sub-groups. Random number selection = random sampling.

bronze.display: River velocity readings (m/s): 0.3, 0.5, 0.4, 0.6, 5.2, 0.5, 0.4. Which value is most likely an anomaly?

misconceptions.message: The anomaly is the value that doesn't fit the pattern. Most values are 0.3–0.6, so 5.2 is far too high — likely a recording error or unusual site.
Don't calculate the mean — just look for the value that stands out. 5.2 is over 10× larger than the others.

bronze.display: A student needs to survey environmental quality at 30 sites in a town that has three distinct zones: town centre, suburbs, and industrial area. Which sampling method should they use?

misconceptions.message: With three distinct zones, stratified sampling ensures each zone is represented proportionally. Random might over-sample one zone.
Systematic (regular intervals) could miss a zone entirely. Stratified sampling takes proportional samples from each zone.

bronze.display: A beach profile survey measures beach height every 5 metres from the sea to the cliff. The student records: 0.2, 0.8, 1.5, 2.3, 3.1, 3.8, 4.5 metres. Are there any anomalies?
options: No — the values show a steady increase as expected

misconceptions.message: Beach profiles are expected to rise from sea to cliff. A steady increase is normal — no anomalies here.
4.5 m at the cliff end is expected. Beach height increases with distance from the sea.

bronze.display: Give ONE reason why a larger sample size produces more reliable results in geographical fieldwork.
options: Larger samples reduce the effect of anomalies on the overall results
Larger samples are always cheaper to collect
Larger samples don't require a sampling method
Larger samples guarantee no measurement errors

misconceptions.message: Larger samples don't eliminate errors — they reduce the impact of any single anomaly on the overall pattern, making results more representative.
Larger samples are usually more expensive and time-consuming, but they're more reliable because anomalies have less impact.

bronze.display: Pebble roundness scores (1–6) at a beach: 2, 3, 2, 4, 3, 2, 9, 3, 2. The scale only goes to 6. What can you say about the value 9?
options: It is a valid high measurement
It is an anomaly — likely a recording error since the scale maximum is 6
It shows the beach has very round pebbles
It should be kept because removing data is never appropriate

misconceptions.message: A score of 9 on a 1–6 scale is impossible — it must be a recording error. This is an anomaly that should be investigated and corrected or removed.
9 exceeds the maximum score of 6, so it cannot be a valid measurement. It's a recording error.

bronze.display: A student places quadrats every 2 metres along a transect from the edge of a footpath into a field. What TWO things is the student investigating?
options: How vegetation changes with distance from the path
How soil type affects building materials
How weather changes across the field

misconceptions.message: Quadrats measure vegetation. A transect from a footpath investigates how vegetation changes with distance from the path (trampling effect).
Quadrats are used for vegetation surveys. Moving away from a footpath tests the impact of trampling on plant life.

silver.display: A town has 4 wards with populations: Ward A = 5,000, Ward B = 10,000, Ward C = 3,000, Ward D = 2,000. A stratified sample of 100 people is needed. How many people should be sampled from Ward B?

misconceptions.message: Stratified means proportional. Total population = 20,000. Ward B proportion = 10,000 ÷ 20,000 = 50%. Sample = 50% of 100 = 50 people.
Ward B is 10,000 out of 20,000 total = 50%. 50% of 100 samples = 50.

silver.display: A student repeats river width measurements 3 times at each site and gets: Site 1: 3.2, 3.4, 3.3; Site 2: 4.1, 2.8, 4.0; Site 3: 5.5, 5.6, 5.4. Which site has the least reliable measurements?

misconceptions.message: Reliability is about consistency of repeated measurements, not the size of the value. Site 2 has the largest range (1.3), showing the most variation — least reliable.
The largest range = least reliable. Site 2 has a range of 4.1 − 2.8 = 1.3 — much more variation than Sites 1 and 3.

silver.display: A student wants to compare pedestrian counts in a city centre at different times of day. They count pedestrians for 5 minutes at 9am, 12pm, 3pm, and 6pm. What type of sampling is this?

misconceptions.message: Sampling at regular time intervals (every 3 hours) is systematic. Stratified would divide by groups (e.g. age, gender) and sample proportionally.
The times are equally spaced (every 3 hours), making this systematic, not random.

silver.hint: Remove 120, add the remaining 8 values, divide by 8
silver.display: Traffic count data at a junction: 45, 52, 48, 51, 47, 53, 120, 49, 46. Calculate the mean with and without the anomaly (120). What is the mean WITHOUT the anomaly? Round to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: You removed one value, so divide by 8 (not 9): 391 ÷ 8 = 48.9.

silver.display: A student surveys 60 households in a village with three land use types: residential (50%), farmland (30%), commercial (20%). Using stratified sampling, how many households should be surveyed in the farmland area?

misconceptions.message: Stratified = proportional. Farmland = 30% of 60 = 18 households.
0.3 × 60 = 18 households.

silver.display: A student measures temperature at the same location every day for a month. What type of variable is 'temperature'?

misconceptions.message: Temperature can take any value on a continuous scale (e.g. 15.3°C, 15.37°C). It's continuous, not discrete (discrete values are whole numbers like counts).
Temperature is measured on a number scale — it's quantitative and continuous, not categorical.

silver.display: A fieldwork group collects 50 pebble measurements on a beach. They want to check if beach material gets rounder with distance from the cliff. They measure roundness on a scale of 1 (angular) to 6 (well-rounded). A student suggests finding the mean roundness at each sampling point. Why might the median be better than the mean here?
options: The median is faster to calculate
The data is on an ordinal scale (ranked categories), so the mean may not be meaningful
The median always gives a higher number
The mean cannot be calculated from integers

misconceptions.message: Speed isn't the issue. Roundness scores are ordinal (ranked 1–6) — the intervals between scores aren't necessarily equal, so the mean may be misleading.
The mean can be calculated from integers. The issue is that roundness is ordinal data — ranked categories where the gaps between scores may not be equal.

worked_examples.question: A student surveys 100 people about their travel habits. The town has 60% car users, 25% bus users, and 15% cyclists. How should they stratify the sample?

steps.label: Look for outliers
steps.content: Most values are between 12 and 17 cm. The value 68 cm is far higher than the others — this is the anomaly.

steps.label: Possible cause
steps.content: It could be a recording error (68 instead of 16), a deep pool, or a measurement taken in the wrong location.

worked_examples.question: River depth measurements (cm): 12, 15, 14, 68, 16, 13, 17. Identify the anomaly.
